medical.title: Intensive BP lowering reduces recurrent stroke after intracerebral hemorrhage
medical.summary: Intensive blood pressure-lowering treatment after intracerebral hemorrhage reduces the risk of recurrent stroke without an increase in serious adverse events, according to a study published in the September issue of The Lancet Neurology.

medical.title: Guidelines needed as AI embraced by mental health practices
medical.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are overwhelmingly being used in mental health practices to support administrative tasks, but University of Queensland researchers have found they potentially lack privacy, accuracy and governance safeguards.

medical.title: Hydrogel-grown tumors could speed cancer drug testing, reduce animal use
medical.summary: A review by University of Manchester scientists says sophisticated lab-grown tumors could help fast-track the search for new cancer treatments while reducing reliance on animal testing.

medical.title: Increasing daily steps is as effective as aerobic exercise in managing asthma
medical.summary: For people with moderate to severe asthma, increasing the number of daily steps may be as effective as structured aerobic training sessions for managing the disease. This finding comes from a study led by researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) and published in the journal Pulmonology.

medical.title: Cancer medication helps reduce SIV reservoir, increasing hope for HIV cure
medical.summary: Emory University researchers have provided the first proof of concept in a nonhuman primate model for eliminating HIV-infected cells with venetoclax, a clinically approved cancer medication. Venetoclax effectively targets and blocks Bcl-2, a protein that not only regulates whether cells live or die but also promotes the survival of cancer cells. Similarly, Bcl-2 is a culprit in sustaining HIV cell reservoirs.

medical.title: Uterine ion channels offer potential new target to delay preterm birth
medical.summary: Scientists have found that targeting a particular group of proteins in the uterus muscle (myometrium) can suppress human uterine contractions in laboratory studies and delay preterm birth in a preclinical model.

medical.title: How new moms cope with stressful news may matter more than the news itself, study finds
medical.summary: The ever-changing social, political and economic landscape in many countries has become more tenuous and intense in recent years. Respondents in a 2026 report from the World Economic Forum indicated a prevailing mood of uncertainty, with 50% anticipating a turbulent or stormy outlook on life over the next two years. This negative perception swells to 57% of respondents when looking ahead to the next 10 years.

medical.title: Why does music ease pain? Researchers map the evidence
medical.summary: Many studies have demonstrated that music-based interventions—such as listening to music—can help reduce pain from a variety of conditions like cancer or osteoarthritis, but researchers still do not understand how or why they help. A new review study led by Joke Bradt, Ph.D., a professor in Drexel University's College of Nursing and Health Professions, examined biological, psychological and social mechanisms that may explain the pain-reducing effects of music. The study, recently published in PAIN Reports, identified important gaps that future research on music-based interventions for pain relief should address.

medical.title: Skull bone marrow inflammation marker rises with chronic pain severity
medical.summary: Chronic pain affects almost one-quarter of U.S. adults. Yet, for most people, current treatment approaches provide only limited relief. Recent research has pointed to bone marrow found in the skull as an important site of communication between the brain and the immune system.

medical.title: Identifying patients at lower risk for kidney transplant rejection
medical.summary: A new risk stratification model developed by Northwestern Medicine scientists may help identify patients at lower risk of kidney transplant rejection, informing more personalized treatment and care strategies with fewer adverse side effects, as detailed in a recent study published in Nature Communications.

medical.title: AI-assisted approach helps novice users capture heart ultrasound images and identify aortic stenosis
medical.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers tested an approach that uses artificial intelligence (AI) to help people without previous ultrasound experience capture heart images and identify patients who may have a common and serious heart valve condition.

medical.title: Caregivers of children with cancer engage in culinary medicine classes and coaching in new study
medical.summary: Caregivers play an essential role in helping children maintain adequate nutrition during their cancer treatment. But treatment-related side effects, such as nausea and poor appetite, can make feeding a child particularly challenging. Nutrition priorities also shift throughout treatment and beyond.

medical.title: AI skin cancer detection tools are getting better, but only for people with light skin
medical.summary: Imagine you're getting out of the shower one morning and notice a mole on your thigh that you've never seen before. It's reddish-brown, bumpy and surprisingly large. Is it a benign mole, or is it melanoma?

science.title: Tiny fossils reveal big insights about ant ancestors
science.summary: Two tiny ant fossils recovered in southern Saskatchewan are helping scientists better understand the evolutionary history of modern ants. Ant fossils dating from 72–56 million years ago are rare. What happened to insects such as ants during this period that saw a mass extinction wipe out all non-bird dinosaurs? How did that event reshape their world?

science.title: From peas to potatoes, AI identifies nearly 800 promising plant proteins for food and cosmetics
science.summary: Scientists from Leeds' School of Food Science and Nutrition have developed an advanced AI process that can rapidly identify plant proteins capable of acting as emulsifiers from tens of millions of initial candidates. To date, it has identified nearly 800. The discovery will cut years of costly trial-and-error research and bring the next generation of plant-based foods and cosmetics closer.

science.title: How an unassuming wildflower thrives in salt-laden air that kills other plants
science.summary: On the windswept coasts of Oregon and California lives an unassuming little plant that can withstand salty blasts that kill its inland counterparts. It's called the yellow monkeyflower. Now, researchers are beginning to understand how it manages to thrive in conditions that leave other plants burned, brown and withered.

science.title: Parliamentary motions show growing AI use, with no disclosure from MPs
science.summary: The two research teams have developed and used AI detectors trained on thousands of political motions in Sweden and the UK. What surprised the researchers was not that politicians were using AI—but that not a single one disclosed this openly.

science.title: Iron helped scientists trace Earth's oxygen. Now it's telling a bigger story
science.summary: For decades, scientists have studied iron preserved in ancient rocks to reconstruct how Earth's oceans and atmosphere became rich in oxygen. A new study suggests iron has recorded other major transformations too.

science.title: Satellites spot forest stress two years before bark beetle die-offs become apparent
science.summary: Satellite measurements detected declining photosynthetic activity in Western U.S. forests two years before bark beetle mortality appeared in aerial detection surveys, according to new University of Utah-led research.

science.title: The Arctic melt season is a week longer now than it was in the 1980s, new research on sea ice trends shows
science.summary: Relatively few people have been to the Arctic, and even fewer have set foot in Antarctica. Most people rely on imagination and the media to visualize these landscapes and the ways they are changing.

science.title: Even second graders can reason like scientists—if we ask them the right way
science.summary: When a child asks "Why does a blowfish puff up?" we often jump in with facts. But what if we paused and suggested that they ask instead, "How does a blowfish puff up?" It may seem like splitting hairs, but this small shift in phrasing could help reshape future generations' capacity for reasoning and critical thought in science and beyond.

science.title: Nanoscale multiferroic materials open the path to efficient magnetic memory technology
science.summary: With the rapid spread of cloud computing, artificial intelligence and data centers, global energy consumption is rising to new heights. A promising way to reduce this burden is to develop memory devices that store information magnetically yet are written using electric fields. Magnetic memories are nonvolatile, meaning stored information is retained without a power supply.

environment.title: Gold miners breach a crucial refuge for rescued Sumatran orangutans
environment.summary: JANTHO, Indonesia — Illegal gold miners in Indonesia’s Aceh province have breached a crucial reintroduction forest for critically endangered Sumatran orangutans rescued from the illegal wildlife trade. “The result of our monitoring indicates that maybe dozens of excavators are suspected of operating in the Jantho forest area,” said Afifuddin, campaign and advocacy lead at the […]

environment.title: Superb fairywrens disappearing in Australia’s capital: Conserving insects could help save them
environment.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

environment.title: Recording a rainforest before Indonesia’s new capital changes it
environment.summary: Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries. In the forests around Pemaluan in East Kalimantan, Indonesian Borneo, researchers led by Wendy Erb at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics in the U.S. have placed audio recorders on mountains, beside caves, and among […]

environment.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga
environment.summary: CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

environment.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
environment.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

environment.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
environment.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

environment.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

environment.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

mix_items.title: Tiny fossils reveal big insights about ant ancestors
mix_items.summary: Two tiny ant fossils recovered in southern Saskatchewan are helping scientists better understand the evolutionary history of modern ants. Ant fossils dating from 72–56 million years ago are rare. What happened to insects such as ants during this period that saw a mass extinction wipe out all non-bird dinosaurs? How did that event reshape their world?

mix_items.title: From peas to potatoes, AI identifies nearly 800 promising plant proteins for food and cosmetics
mix_items.summary: Scientists from Leeds' School of Food Science and Nutrition have developed an advanced AI process that can rapidly identify plant proteins capable of acting as emulsifiers from tens of millions of initial candidates. To date, it has identified nearly 800. The discovery will cut years of costly trial-and-error research and bring the next generation of plant-based foods and cosmetics closer.

mix_items.title: How an unassuming wildflower thrives in salt-laden air that kills other plants
mix_items.summary: On the windswept coasts of Oregon and California lives an unassuming little plant that can withstand salty blasts that kill its inland counterparts. It's called the yellow monkeyflower. Now, researchers are beginning to understand how it manages to thrive in conditions that leave other plants burned, brown and withered.

mix_items.title: Parliamentary motions show growing AI use, with no disclosure from MPs
mix_items.summary: The two research teams have developed and used AI detectors trained on thousands of political motions in Sweden and the UK. What surprised the researchers was not that politicians were using AI—but that not a single one disclosed this openly.

mix_items.title: Iron helped scientists trace Earth's oxygen. Now it's telling a bigger story
mix_items.summary: For decades, scientists have studied iron preserved in ancient rocks to reconstruct how Earth's oceans and atmosphere became rich in oxygen. A new study suggests iron has recorded other major transformations too.

mix_items.title: Satellites spot forest stress two years before bark beetle die-offs become apparent
mix_items.summary: Satellite measurements detected declining photosynthetic activity in Western U.S. forests two years before bark beetle mortality appeared in aerial detection surveys, according to new University of Utah-led research.

mix_items.title: The Arctic melt season is a week longer now than it was in the 1980s, new research on sea ice trends shows
mix_items.summary: Relatively few people have been to the Arctic, and even fewer have set foot in Antarctica. Most people rely on imagination and the media to visualize these landscapes and the ways they are changing.

mix_items.title: Even second graders can reason like scientists—if we ask them the right way
mix_items.summary: When a child asks "Why does a blowfish puff up?" we often jump in with facts. But what if we paused and suggested that they ask instead, "How does a blowfish puff up?" It may seem like splitting hairs, but this small shift in phrasing could help reshape future generations' capacity for reasoning and critical thought in science and beyond.

mix_items.title: Nanoscale multiferroic materials open the path to efficient magnetic memory technology
mix_items.summary: With the rapid spread of cloud computing, artificial intelligence and data centers, global energy consumption is rising to new heights. A promising way to reduce this burden is to develop memory devices that store information magnetically yet are written using electric fields. Magnetic memories are nonvolatile, meaning stored information is retained without a power supply.

mix_items.title: Intensive BP lowering reduces recurrent stroke after intracerebral hemorrhage
mix_items.summary: Intensive blood pressure-lowering treatment after intracerebral hemorrhage reduces the risk of recurrent stroke without an increase in serious adverse events, according to a study published in the September issue of The Lancet Neurology.

mix_items.title: Guidelines needed as AI embraced by mental health practices
mix_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are overwhelmingly being used in mental health practices to support administrative tasks, but University of Queensland researchers have found they potentially lack privacy, accuracy and governance safeguards.

mix_items.title: Hydrogel-grown tumors could speed cancer drug testing, reduce animal use
mix_items.summary: A review by University of Manchester scientists says sophisticated lab-grown tumors could help fast-track the search for new cancer treatments while reducing reliance on animal testing.

mix_items.title: Increasing daily steps is as effective as aerobic exercise in managing asthma
mix_items.summary: For people with moderate to severe asthma, increasing the number of daily steps may be as effective as structured aerobic training sessions for managing the disease. This finding comes from a study led by researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) and published in the journal Pulmonology.

mix_items.title: Cancer medication helps reduce SIV reservoir, increasing hope for HIV cure
mix_items.summary: Emory University researchers have provided the first proof of concept in a nonhuman primate model for eliminating HIV-infected cells with venetoclax, a clinically approved cancer medication. Venetoclax effectively targets and blocks Bcl-2, a protein that not only regulates whether cells live or die but also promotes the survival of cancer cells. Similarly, Bcl-2 is a culprit in sustaining HIV cell reservoirs.

mix_items.title: Uterine ion channels offer potential new target to delay preterm birth
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that targeting a particular group of proteins in the uterus muscle (myometrium) can suppress human uterine contractions in laboratory studies and delay preterm birth in a preclinical model.

mix_items.title: How new moms cope with stressful news may matter more than the news itself, study finds
mix_items.summary: The ever-changing social, political and economic landscape in many countries has become more tenuous and intense in recent years. Respondents in a 2026 report from the World Economic Forum indicated a prevailing mood of uncertainty, with 50% anticipating a turbulent or stormy outlook on life over the next two years. This negative perception swells to 57% of respondents when looking ahead to the next 10 years.

mix_items.title: Why does music ease pain? Researchers map the evidence
mix_items.summary: Many studies have demonstrated that music-based interventions—such as listening to music—can help reduce pain from a variety of conditions like cancer or osteoarthritis, but researchers still do not understand how or why they help. A new review study led by Joke Bradt, Ph.D., a professor in Drexel University's College of Nursing and Health Professions, examined biological, psychological and social mechanisms that may explain the pain-reducing effects of music. The study, recently published in PAIN Reports, identified important gaps that future research on music-based interventions for pain relief should address.

mix_items.title: Skull bone marrow inflammation marker rises with chronic pain severity
mix_items.summary: Chronic pain affects almost one-quarter of U.S. adults. Yet, for most people, current treatment approaches provide only limited relief. Recent research has pointed to bone marrow found in the skull as an important site of communication between the brain and the immune system.

mix_items.title: Identifying patients at lower risk for kidney transplant rejection
mix_items.summary: A new risk stratification model developed by Northwestern Medicine scientists may help identify patients at lower risk of kidney transplant rejection, informing more personalized treatment and care strategies with fewer adverse side effects, as detailed in a recent study published in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: AI-assisted approach helps novice users capture heart ultrasound images and identify aortic stenosis
mix_items.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers tested an approach that uses artificial intelligence (AI) to help people without previous ultrasound experience capture heart images and identify patients who may have a common and serious heart valve condition.

mix_items.title: Caregivers of children with cancer engage in culinary medicine classes and coaching in new study
mix_items.summary: Caregivers play an essential role in helping children maintain adequate nutrition during their cancer treatment. But treatment-related side effects, such as nausea and poor appetite, can make feeding a child particularly challenging. Nutrition priorities also shift throughout treatment and beyond.

mix_items.title: AI skin cancer detection tools are getting better, but only for people with light skin
mix_items.summary: Imagine you're getting out of the shower one morning and notice a mole on your thigh that you've never seen before. It's reddish-brown, bumpy and surprisingly large. Is it a benign mole, or is it melanoma?

mix_items.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

mix_items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
mix_items.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

mix_items.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
mix_items.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

mix_items.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

mix_items.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.
